title: The filter at 3 a.m.
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative; every rate and target comes from the prescriber’s order and the unit’s CRRT protocol.
intro: You are the ICU nurse caring for Mr. Edgar Villanueva, 61, with septic shock and acute kidney injury, on continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) with regional citrate anticoagulation through a right femoral catheter. His order is a patient total balance of 100 mL negative per hour. At midnight you notice that the transmembrane pressure and the pressure drop across the filter have been climbing for four hours.

choices.text: Check the citrate and calcium lines, look at the filter, report the trend, and plan a change.
choices.feedback: A transmembrane pressure or pressure drop climbing over hours predicts clotting long before the circuit stops. That gives you time for a controlled change that returns the blood, instead of losing the circuit.

choices.text: Wait for the machine to alarm before doing anything.
choices.feedback: A rising trend is a warning you can act on. A clotted circuit is a loss you can only record.

choices.text: Increase the blood flow a little to push through the forming clot, and recheck the pressures in an hour.
choices.feedback: Blood flow changes follow the order and protocol. Check the anticoagulation and report the trend first.
choices.then: You check the infusions, report the trend, and plan a change.

n2.scene: At 01:40 Mr. Villanueva, now waking more, says his fingers and lips are tingling. His pressure has fallen to 92/54 and the monitor shows a longer QT interval.

choices.text: The calcium infusion. It is empty: replace it, report, and send an ionized calcium.
choices.feedback: On citrate, the calcium bag is as important as the citrate bag. Tingling, spasm, falling pressure, and a long QT point to low ionized calcium, and a calcium bag that ran dry unnoticed is a common cause.

choices.text: Increase the citrate rate, since the filter has been clotting and better anticoagulation will protect the new circuit.
choices.feedback: More citrate binds more calcium and makes his low calcium worse. Never adjust citrate without knowing the patient’s ionized calcium.
choices.then: You stop and check the calcium infusion: the bag is empty. You replace it per protocol and report.

choices.text: Give a fluid bolus for the low pressure.
choices.feedback: The cause is likely the calcium, not volume. Check the calcium infusion first.
choices.then: You check: the calcium bag is empty. You replace it and report.

n3.scene: Before the planned change could be made, the circuit clots at 03:00. The return pressure is very high and the filter is dark.

choices.text: No; protocol forbids it. Record the estimated loss and report.
choices.feedback: Returning blood through a clotted circuit can send clot into the patient. The loss is recorded and reported; in an anemic ICU patient it matters.

choices.text: Yes: return the blood slowly by hand, since he is anemic and cannot afford to lose the volume in the circuit.
choices.feedback: Forcing a return through clot risks embolizing clot into the patient. Follow the protocol.
choices.then: You stop, discard the circuit per protocol, and record the estimated loss.

choices.text: Ask the physician first before doing anything.
choices.feedback: Reporting is right, but know your protocol: blood is not returned from a clotted circuit.

n4.scene: In the 04:00–05:00 hour on the new circuit, the machine removed 200 mL net. His intake was 260 mL (infusions, feed, flushes) and his output 30 mL (urine and drain). The order is 100 mL negative per hour.
n4.prompt: What was his patient total balance?

choices.text: +30 mL (260 − 30 − 200), 130 short of the goal; act per order and record.
choices.feedback: The machine balances only its own bags. Patient total balance is everything in minus everything out, including the machine’s net removal.

choices.text: 200 mL negative: the machine removed exactly the 200 mL it was set to remove this hour.
choices.feedback: That is the machine’s number. The machine knows nothing about the infusions, the feed, or the urine bag.
He was 30 mL positive, 130 mL away from the goal in one hour. Over a day that becomes liters.

n5.scene: At 06:00 a new antibiotic is ordered, and the physician also plans to raise the effluent rate. His temperature reads 36.8 °C.

choices.text: Ask whether the dose is adjusted for CRRT; note the downtime; fever may be hidden.
choices.feedback: Continuous therapy removes many antibiotics. Under-dosing in sepsis is as dangerous as overdosing. Cooled blood can mask fever, so look for other signs of infection.

choices.text: Give it as written; dosing is the doctor’s job.
choices.feedback: Dosing is the prescriber’s, but asking whether it accounts for CRRT is part of safe administration.

choices.text: Give it as written, and note his normal temperature in the handover as a sign the infection is improving.
choices.feedback: On CRRT, a normal temperature may be the circuit cooling him. Look at the white count, lactate, and pressures, and ask about the dose.

end.title: Handover
end.text: At handover you report the clotted circuit and estimated blood loss, the empty calcium bag and its correction, the ionized calcium result, the cumulative balance against the goal, and the antibiotic dose check. The unit adds “calcium bag level” to the hourly CRRT checks.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Act on the trend: rising TMP or pressure drop means plan a change before the circuit clots.
  • On citrate, never let the calcium bag run dry. Tingling, hypotension, and a long QT: check the calcium first.
  • No blood return from a clotted circuit; record the loss.
  • The machine balances its bags; you balance the patient.
  • Ask about drug dosing on CRRT; fever may be hidden.

See Anticoagulation, Fluid balance, The circuit and Complications.
